item.content:encoded:
Inside ShareChat’s Mixed FY26

ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech delivered some hits and some misses in FY26. While the homegrown social media giant crossed the ₹1,000 Cr revenue mark and found a new growth engine in microdramas, what played the spoilsport were losses and surging expenses.

Here is a quick look at Mohalla Tech’s FY26 numbers:

  • Operating revenue zoomed 40.4% YoY to ₹1,016.3 Cr
  • Net loss widened 78.5% YoY to ₹1,978.4 Cr
  • Total expenses surged 65.6% YoY to ₹3,083 Cr

Loss Widens: Mohalla Tech’s FY26 losses were largely driven by rising expenses. Employee benefit costs more than doubled YoY in the fiscal under review, while forex losses also surged following Rupee’s depreciation. Meanwhile, marketing and user acquisition spending also jumped nearly 8X YoY as Mohalla Tech invested aggressively in growth.

The Microdrama Pivot: The launch of QuickTV opened a crucial new revenue stream and generated nearly a third of Mohalla Tech’s total income in FY26. This pivot helped buffer against advertising headwinds in the aftermath of the ban on real-money gaming last year. But the unit economics of microdramas remained challenging, forcing the platform to rely heavily on ad-supported models to mint revenues.

The EBITDA Turnaround: Despite the widening losses, Mohalla Tech’s operating performance showed improvement. The startup halved its FY26 EBITDA loss YoY to ₹91 Cr, suggesting that its core business is inching closer to profitability. The management also claimed that the startup posted its first EBITDA-positive quarter in Q1 FY27 due to better monetisation across subscriptions, livestreaming and advertising. 

The FY27 Test: Mohalla Tech is now targeting an EBITDA profit of ₹25 Cr in FY27, and claims to have already reported around ₹740 Cr in revenue in H1 FY27. The management now expects advertising to rebound strongly, with AVOD top line projected to cross ₹350 Cr in the ongoing fiscal. The startup remains little optimistic about subscriptions, believing most Indian users will not pay for microdramas and that paying users will remain below 100 Mn even as the market matures.

As ShareChat taps into microdramas to finally build a durable business, here is all about how parent Mohalla Tech fared on the financial front in FY26…

From The Editor’s Desk

MakeMyTrip All Set For IPO

  • The Nasdaq-listed online travel aggregator’s India arm has received SEBI’s approval to launch its IPO in the country. This comes four months after MMT filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI in July this year.
  • The issue is expected to consist entirely of an offer for sale component worth $1 Bn, with no fresh issue of shares. MMT India will continue to remain a subsidiary of the US-listed entity following the IPO. 
  • MakeMyTrip listed on the Nasdaq in 2010 due to the maturity of the US tech ecosystem. However, since then, the Indian new-age tech landscape has grown to house over 70 listed startups, which have raised billions of dollars from their respective IPOs. 

Casualties At Tata’s iPhone Factory

  • Three workers died of asphyxiation during maintenance work at Tata’s iPhone component manufacturing unit in Tamil Nadu’s Hosur. The incident took place inside a nano-filtration feed tank, operated by US-based Ecolab’s subsidiary Nalco Water.
  • While the preliminary probe suggests toxic smoke inhalation, sources added that there were no proper safety measures in place. 
  • Tata Electronics is now expected to face an investigation by a joint team of officials from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board and the state’s Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health.

InMobi’s New Marketing Move

  • The IPO-bound adtech unicorn has paid ₹65 Cr (excluding GST) to secure the naming rights for Bengaluru’s Ibbaluru metro station for a period of 30 years. With this, the station will now be called InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station.
  • The sum will go towards Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation Ltd’s non-fare revenue. The BMRCL also expects the partnership to encourage higher corporate participation in the city’s public transport ecosystem.
  • The deal comes as InMobi’s IPO continues to be in limbo. Last heard, the startup was eyeing a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. While the unicorn has roped in four bankers to helm its public issue, InMobi is yet to file its DRHP.

Sarvam Ropes In Ex-Google Exec

  • The AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as its new president and chief business officer. He will also join the startup’s board of directors.
  • With more than 35 years of experience under his belt, Sreedharan has previously worked at big tech giants like Google India, Microsoft India and IBM. He previously also served at Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others.
  • His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to build a larger enterprise AI business and strengthen its client roster. Founded in 2023, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, compute infrastructure and enterprise AI tools. It has raised $380 Mn to date.

Google Backs Froncort.AI

  • The healthtech startup has raised $2.3 Mn from the big tech giant’s philanthropic arm, Google.org, to scale its AI-powered disease surveillance and detection platform. The support also includes $200K in Google Cloud credits and technical expertise.
  • Founded in 2024, Froncort leverages AI, satellite imagery and health data to identify areas with higher prevalence of infectious diseases like tuberculosis. It also guides health workers with dedicated routes to enable targeted screenings.
  • The funding comes as the AI sector is attracting a growing share of investor capital, driven by novel solutions, enterprise AI use cases and a thriving local talent base. As per Inc42 data, AI funding in India grew 265% YoY to $438 Mn in Q3 2026.

Matrimony’s Q2 Show

  • The listed matchmaking platform’s consolidated net profit skyrocketed 165.4% YoY to ₹20.7 Cr in Q2 FY27. This came on the back of expanding margins, a tighter leash on expenses and operating revenue rising 17.6% YoY to ₹134.8 Cr.
  • On the operational front, Matrimony added 3.02 Lakh paid subscribers to its kitty in Q2 FY27, up 27% YoY. The matchmaking vertical also saw its reported billings jump nearly 11% YoY to ₹130 Cr in the quarter under review. 
  • The listed company also said that its board approved the acquisition of an additional 50% stake in astrology-based matchmaking platform, Astro-Vision, for ₹8 Cr. Post the deal, Matrimony’s stake in the startup will rise to 76.9%.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

Legacy Equipment Enters The Unmanned Era

Automation often means buying expensive new robots and redesigning operations around them. Hyderabad-based TensrAI is trying to flip this model by retrofitting existing industrial equipment with autonomous capabilities.

Built For Automation: Founded in 2022, TensrAI is building a unified autonomy platform for industrial and commercial robots, vehicles and machines. Its stack combines camera-first navigation, AI-based localisation, vision-language-model reasoning and autonomous mobility. It is also developing a mobile manipulator for handling materials and performing other tasks.

A Retrofit-First Stack: The startup’s AI stack is designed to help equipment perceive surroundings, interpret instructions, navigate changing spaces and perform work with limited human intervention. TensrAI initially plans to target factories, warehouses, airports, hospitals, malls and commercial campuses. 

The Road Ahead: TensrAI’s retrofit approach is intended to reduce the cost and complexity of adopting robotics. But the startup will have to prove that its autonomy stack can work reliably across machines, environments and real-world tasks. With India’s robotics market projected to become a $4.6 Bn opportunity by 2030, can TensrAI make retrofitting autonomy easy for Indian factories?

From spacetech to semiconductors, Indian VC firms are backing startups building some of India’s most ambitious technologies. Here is a closer look at where the money is going and what India’s next wave of deeptech innovation looks like…

item.title: GoKwik’s Golden Handcuffs: Non-Compete Clause Puts Vested ESOPs In Jeopardy
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Employee stock options (ESOPs) have become a major talking point in India’s startup ecosystem this year, with questions around liquidity,…
item.content:encoded:
Employee stock options (ESOPs) have become a major talking point in India’s startup ecosystem this year, with questions around liquidity, employee wealth creation and the ability to monetise years of accumulated stock options taking centre stage. While Flipkart’s ESOP-related  employee woes have been in the news all through this summer, digital commerce startup GoKwik has brought another dimension to the ESOP debate.

GoKwik, which is backed by the likes of Z47 Partners, Peak XV Partners, RTP Global and Think Investments, has amended its existing ESOP Plan 2021, through the insertion of a new non-compete clause, naming nine companies that employees are barred from joining or associating with, if they want to retain their ESOP rights. 

The provision gives the startup the authority to revoke unvested and vested-but-unexercised employee stock options if employees (even those who have quit GoKwik) are found to have breached the restriction. 

Inc42 has seen a copy of the internal document in question which has caused consternation among current and former employees. The mail was also sent to former GoKwik employees who continue to hold options. 

The insertion of the clause has raised questions around employee mobility and the rights of existing ESOP holders, particularly as the new provision applies to options granted in the past as well as future stock options.

The clause was communicated to employees in the month of August, amid a spate of senior-level exits. The exits include vice president Sneha Rao, Sharad Gupta, the senior director of product management for the Checkout business, and Siddhartha Bahl, head of product, among others.

The policy lists Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo (acquired by Pine Labs), and Pine Labs as competing businesses. 

Under the provision, employees cannot accept employment with, render services to, advise, invest in or otherwise associate with these companies. If the company determines that an employee has breached the restriction, it can forfeit their unvested options as well as vested options that have not yet been exercised.

The GoKwik ESOP Plan 2021 (“Plan”) allows GoKwik to cancel or forfeit both unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if the Board or Nomination and Remuneration Committee determines that an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”.

While unvested options are stock options that employees are not yet entitled to exercise, vested-but-unexercised options are those that employees are entitled to exercise but have not yet converted into shares. The provision does not affect ESOPs that have already been exercised.

In effect, an employee joining a competing business could lose options that are yet to vest, as well as those that have already vested by have not been exercised. This means that even employees who completed the vesting period and earned the right to buy shares coils lose those options if the company determines that they have breached the competition restriction. However, options already exercised and converted into shares are not covered by this forfeiture provision. 

Importantly, the restriction applies to all grants, whether issued before or after its effective date, and continues to bind former employees holding vested options even after their employment ends.

The restriction, however, is not indefinite. A special resolution passed by GoKwik shareholders at the company’s September, 2025 AGM provides that the competition related restriction will remain in force from the grant date until two years after an employee;s last date of employment or engagement with the company or its affiliates. In other words, the restriction applies throughout an employee’s tenure at GoKwik and continues for two years after their departure. During this period, joining or associating with a competing business could put their outstanding ESOPs at risk.

The policy appears to carve out passive investments in publicly traded securities. It also allows the GoKwik Board to approve exceptions in writing, with employees required to write to the company for such deviations.

The inclusion is significant because it directly links an employee’s association with named competitors to the potential loss of their stock options, including options that have already vested but remain unexercised.

Questions sent to GoKwik didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story even after Inc42 extended the deadline for responses upon the company’s request. 

Instead, GoKwik issued a press release claiming former employees might get 9X average returns on their ESOPs and the startup has turned EBITDA positive in October 2026. But this press release does not mention any of the concerns that employees have brought up.

Employees In Limbo 

“The sudden change in the ESOP policy was a shock. People who have quite a significant ESOP holding are all of a sudden in fear that they will lose it if they leave the company and try to join a better company. Now the names that they have mentioned are much superior companies that they would want to join as part of having a better career trajectory,” a former GoKwik employee told Inc42.

Employees with significant ESOP holdings, particularly those who may consider moving to other companies in the same sector, are stuck in limbo. 

Sources in the company say they are weighing potential job opportunities against the potential loss from forfeiting their outstanding stock options. This is especially relevant for employees whose options have vested but have not been exercised, since the new clause explicitly includes vested-but-unexercised options within the scope of potential forfeiture.

The forfeiture, however, is not automatic. The Board or the Nomination and Remuneration Committee has the discretion to determine whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach” and decide whether to cancel or forfeit their unvested and/or vested-but-unexercised options. 

Worryingly for employees, the provision is ambiguous about what kind of relationships are covered. For instance, it says that ESOPs may be revoked for employees who may “otherwise associate” with a competing business. This could cover relationships beyond direct employment, and the policy does not make the scope of this phrase immediately clear.

The timing of the amendment is also notable against the backdrop of GoKwik’s growth ambitions and recent senior-level departures as well as layoffs. 

Founded in 2020 by Chirag Taneja, Vivek Bajpai, and Ankush Talwar, GoKwik is an ecommerce enablement startup that offers software tools to help online brands improve checkout, reduce order returns, automate customer engagement and increase sales. Earlier this year, Inc42 exclusively reported that GoKwik had laid off around 120 employees.

The startup has to date raised $68 Mn in funding and counts investors including Peak XV Partners, Z47 Partners, RTP Global, and Think Investments, among others.

In an interview with BW Disrupt, published in July 2025, cofounder and CEO Taneja said the company generated around ₹250 Cr in revenue in FY25. However, GoKwik Commerce Solutions Pvt Ltd’s financial disclosures show consolidated operating revenue of ₹146.2 Cr for FY25, and total consolidated revenue of approximately ₹163 Cr. GoKwik did not respond to questions about this discrepancy. 

Among the nine companies named in the policy, GoKwik directly competes with the likes of Shiprocket’s Fastrr, Razorpay’s Magic Checkout, Shopflo, and Cashfree’s One Click Checkout, while the remaining companies operate in adjacent or overlapping segments of ecommerce enablement, fintech, and merchant services ecosystem.

Making Sense Of Non-Compete For ESOPs

Non-compete restrictions are commonly included in employment agreements in India, although their enforceability is difficult to establish. 

However, explicitly naming competitors in an ESOP policy and linking an employee’s association with them to the cancellation of vested-but-unexercised options is unusual, according to Siddharth Manchanda, Partner at JSA Advocates & Solicitors. Manchanda further clarified that his comments reflected a general understanding of the law and should not be construed as an opinion on GoKwik.

He also said that a restriction on an ESOP policy is unusual but its substance is not entirely new. Most ESOP policies, in his view, contain provisions that allow options to lapse if an employee breaches their employment agreement. 

Since employment agreements commonly include non-compete restrictions, companies may already have an indirect route to link an employee joining a competitor with the loss of ESOPs.

However, companies do not typically go after employees solely for joining a competitor, unless the situation also involves allegations of confidentiality breaches, data theft or misuse of proprietary information. 

Under Rule 12(8)(f) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, unvested options ordinarily expire upon resignation or termination, while vested options can be exercised within the period specified by the ESOP scheme. 

The more consequential question, according to Manchanda, is whether a company can introduce additional grounds for forfeiture after employees have already received their options. While employers have discretion to set the grounds for cancellation when drafting an ESOP policy, changing those terms later to employees’ disadvantage could be legally questionable.

In GoKwik’s case, the amendment applies to options that were already outstanding.

As per another lawyer Inc42 spoke to, this change could be challenged from a legal standpoint, as amendments that adversely affect employees’ existing ESOP rights raise questions around their validity. He added that the enforceability of non-compete restrictions and the cancellation of ESOPs on that basis remains an unsettled issue that could be tested in legal dispute.

ESOPs Turn Into A Governance Question

The clause also raises a governance question that goes beyond enforceability. Plus, some clauses in the changed policy are ambiguous at best. 

Under the plan, it is the Board or its Nomination and Remuneration Committee that decides whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”, a decision in which employees, and the former employees the clause continues to bind, have no part.

ESOPs are a critical lever when it comes to attracting employees to early stage startups. They stand in for salary. An early stage startup can’t match what IT services giants, multinationals or global capability centres (GCCs) pay. 

Stock options fill the gap. The employee takes a lower monthly salary in exchange for a share of the upside in the future. At that stage the ESOP is part of the offer, not a perk.

ESOPs are also seen as a retention tactic. Options vest over time and it ties in employees to the success of the business in the long run. Leaving early means giving up the options that haven’t vested or even leaving money on the table.

And finally, ESOPs are one wealth creation instrument in the hands of employers. A total of 12 startups executed ESOP buybacks in 2025, paying ₹1,409 Cr ($158 Mn) to more than 9,200 employees. In 2024, 23 startups paid out ₹1,448 Cr to employees through buybacks. 

Even a minor change in the ESOP policy can lead to employees having to sacrifice an amount that can be equivalent to years of salary. 

GoKwik would not be the first startup to change ESOP terms after the options were granted. In December 2025, Unacademy cut the window its former employees had to exercise their vested options from 10 years to 30 days, while it was in M&A talks. Unacademy put the change on hold a month later, after a backlash from former employees. 

GoKwik’s claim of 9X average returns for former employees tells us what the options may be worth, but do employees get to keep them?

GoKwik’s handling of the issue will be tested the first time an employee with vested options joins one of the nine companies it names, unless, like Unacademy, the ecommerce company decides to revisit this provision before then.

Until that happens, every employee holding ESOPs, current or former, is left with the question: does a vested option actually belong to them even if it has been allocated on paper, or is it only theirs for as long as they stay away from the companies that GoKwik bars?

Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam
Creatives: Varshita Srivastava

item.title: SoftBank Q2: Lenskart & Meesho Drive Valuation Gains, Ola Electric Books Losses
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Japanese tech investor SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2 (SVF2) booked a valuation loss of $42 Mn on its investment in listed…
item.content:encoded:
Japanese tech investor SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2 (SVF2) booked a valuation loss of $42 Mn on its investment in listed Indian electric vehicle (EV) maker Ola Electric in the quarter ended September 2026 (Q2 FY26 as per the investment firm’s nomenclature).

In its investor presentation, SoftBank said that the EV manufacturer’s gross return to the SVF2 stood at $370 Mn in the quarter under review, down $42 Mn (or 10.2%) from $412 Mn in the preceding Q1 FY26. 

The latest gross return figures are almost 30% lower than $556 Mn that the fund claims to have invested in the OEM so far. 

In contrast, other listed Indian startups in SVF2’s portfolio – Lenskart and Meesho – together contributed valuation gains worth $394 Mn to the fund’s kitty in Q2 FY26.

SoftBank said that the Indian omnichannel eyewear giant helped SVF2 rake in an additional $273 Mn in gross returns during the quarter under review. With this, the fund’s total gross gains from Lenskart stood at $1.3 Bn in Q2 FY26, up 27% sequentially from $1 Bn in preceding quarter. 

On similar lines, Meesho added another $121 Mn in gains to SVF2’s corpus in the quarter under review. Overall, the Japanese tech giant’s fund sat on gross gains worth $642 Mn on account of the homegrown ecommerce giant in Q2 FY26, up from $521 Mn in the previous quarter.

“The investment gain at SVF2 reflected increases in the fair values of certain private portfolio companies due to higher valuations in recent transactions as well as higher share prices of certain public portfolio companies, including Meesho Limited and Lenskart Solutions Limited,” added SoftBank in a statement.

SoftBank claims to have so far invested $225 Mn and $285 Mn in Lenskart and Meesho, respectively.

Meanwhile, another homegrown SVF2 portfolio startup Swiggy saw a valuation gain of nearly $14 Mn in the quarter under review. The foodtech giant minted gross returns worth $451 Mn in Q2 FY26 (up from $437 Mn in Q1 FY26) against a total investment of $450 Mn.

However, the road was not so smooth for listed Indian startups in Vision Fund 1 (SVF1). The fund booked a sequential valuation loss of $34 Mn on account of Delhivery in Q2 FY26. Against a gross return of $701 Mn in Q1 FY26, the logistics giant ended the September 2026 quarter with an even lower gross return of $667 Mn.

Similarly, SoftBank pegged the gross return on its investment in FirstCry parent BrainBees Solutions at $308 Mn in the quarter under review, down 14% or $50 Mn, from $358 Mn in Q1 FY26.

Overall, SoftBank swung to the red and posted a net loss of nearly $7 Bn in Q2 FY26 against a profit of $15.9 Bn in the year ago period. This was its first loss-making quarter in nearly two years as the company was hit by rising buildout costs for data centres in the US and a sharp jump in financing payments.

The investment firm also reported $14.1 Bn in net sales in the quarter under review, up 15.6% from $12.2 Bn in Q2 FY25. 

SoftBank is one of the major foreign investors in the country and has so far deployed nearly $16 Bn in Indian startups. Having funded nearly a fifth of India’s 100+ unicorns, SoftBank has previously backed the likes of Flipkart, OYO, Delhivery, OfBusiness, FirstCry and Meesho.

item.title: NVIDIA Scandal & AI Selloff In the US: India’s Neocloud Boom Faces Twin Tests
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: The alleged espionage scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and the growing scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings with China…
item.content:encoded:
The alleged espionage scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and the growing scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings with China have added another layer of uncertainty to the global AI infrastructure market already facing questions about its financing model.  

At the same time, political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could slow infrastructure investment, putting pressure on companies that have borrowed heavily to build capacity.

While unrelated, these developments present two separate risks to the investment model underpinning the AI infrastructure boom.

The first is already visible in the American stock market. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN witnessing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on.

The selloff has only intensified talk of an AI bubble, and neoclouds in India face the risk of getting caught in the middle. 

Neoclouds – AI infrastructure providers that offer GPU-as-a-service – have emerged as an important part of NVIDIA’s AI ecosystem. They provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. 

Neocloud business models are capital-intensive, with GPU procurement, data centre capacity, and financing arrangements determining how quickly they can scale up. NVIDIA has played a significant role in supporting this ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements, helping expand the market for its chips beyond traditional hyperscalers. India is increasingly becoming part of this infrastructure buildout.

That buildout serves two demand pools. One is subsidised compute for domestic startups, researchers and institutions under the IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. The other is commercial workloads from customers willing to pay for guaranteed capacity. The first highlights the scale of the government programme, but sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage. To justify their spending, India’s neoclouds are betting on the second.

Among the main Indian players, Yotta plans to spend over $7 Bn on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 Bn IPO, partly to repay debt. ESDS went to the market after the cost of the GPU servers it planned to buy rose from ₹25 Lakh to ₹1.8 Cr. E2E Networks, meanwhile, reported a 411% year-on-year jump in Q2 revenue.

Besides these, the likes of NxtGen, NeevCloud and Neysa are also building their neocloud infrastructure in India in anticipation of a big adoption wave. 

US giant CoreWeave is also entering India as the sole tenant of a planned 240 MW AdaniConneX data centre campus. However, any sustained pressure on its financing or expansion plans could have implications for the project. 

If concerns in the US around data centre build-up trickle down to India, neoclouds will be one of the first to get hit as a lot of their build-up depends on institutional funding commitment. The question is whether Indian companies will continue to enjoy the financial backing and attract customer commitments to withstand the headwinds if and when they come.

No Anchor Customers In India

The investment case for US AI infrastructure companies is underpinned by large customers such as Meta and OpenAI, whose scale and long-term compute requirements offer some visibility into future demand. These anchor customers make it easier for infrastructure providers to secure financing and justify large upfront investments.

Indian neoclouds, however, do not yet have comparable customer base to underwrite their expansion plans. International customers now account for 75-80% of Yotta’s customer base, partly because they are willing to pay more. Within India, however, the IndiaAI Mission is emerging as an important source of demand, although it utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 Cr, which has directly impacted hardware procurement and deployment timelines, as Neysa mentioned in one of its blogs. 

A recent Moneycontrol report highlighted a mismatch in the Indian market: some GPUs are underused, while startups and researchers say fragmented capacity, allocation delays and the type of hardware on offer can make suitable compute difficult to obtain. A headline GPU count may therefore obscure both the quality of available clusters and the path from allocation to actual use. 

The mismatch makes domestic demand hard to read. The demand exists, but it does not always reach the neoclouds that have built capacity for it. Even well-funded companies are waiting. Juspay, which buys GPUs with its own cash, has been “given commitments that it will take three to six months” to receive them, co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said at a media briefing. When large customers buy and run their own hardware, and smaller ones struggle to find suitable clusters, aggregate capacity figures say little about how much will turn into long-term, paying contracts for neoclouds. 

Can government-backed compute requirements offer the kind of long-term revenue visibility that hyperscaler contracts provide in the US? Or will Indian neoclouds remain dependent on international customers to sustain utilisation and justify their infrastructure investments?

GPU infrastructure requires substantial upfront capital, while the returns depend on sustained utilisation, predictable demand and long-term customer commitments. Notably, government-led regulations as well as citizen pushback could limit data centre build; it even emerged as a major factor for voters in the recent US midterm elections. For Indian neocloud players, which are increasingly catering to foreign and especially US-based clients, could suffer a trickle-down effect. Neocloud stocks, those of Coreweave, Nebius and Iren, among others, battered after the Democratic win in the recent elections. 

Closer home, ESDS and E2E stocks are already suffering from the second order impact of the sharp selloff in US tech stocks, following the mid-term results. On November 9, ESDS closed at approximately ₹1,147.25, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35, while E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, significantly lower than its October 14 high of ₹769.

The NVIDIA Question

NVIDIA’s role in the neocloud ecosystem goes beyond supplying GPUs. Its investments, financing arrangements and partnerships with infrastructure providers have helped bring new compute capacity online. But the relationship varies across Indian companies.

NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness. Procurement, financing and customer contracts are separate arrangements. The company acknowledged the concentration risk of relying on a single technology provider, but said it ties investments to customer commitments and available financing.

“The market correction reinforces the need for discipline. We assess each project on its commercial viability and phase investments accordingly,” Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, told Inc42. 

ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA. The company buys systems from OEMs and system integrators such as Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. It has also signed a $1.25 Bn, seven-year agreement with Australia’s Sharon AI. Sharon AI owns and operates an 8,000-GPU cluster, which ESDS uses to serve its domestic and global customers. ESDS plans to explore similar partnerships.

“I would separate technology dependence from financial dependence,” said Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS. He pointed out that all of ESDS’s deployed GPU capacity runs on NVIDIA. 

Financing is a different matter. ESDS commits capex only after a customer has paid at least 35% of the project cost, and only then does it place orders with OEMs or system integrators, Somani said.

Both companies say financing for neocloud centres is getting more selective. Lenders and investors now favour projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive.

This is where the economic model gets complicated. NVIDIA has offered neoclouds worldwide a revenue-sharing and credit-support model in July, but later paused some of the deals, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. 

Yotta is exploring similar structures where partners fund and own the GPUs, while the company installs and operates them in its data centres and signs customer contracts. 

Gorilla, the Nasdaq-listed British tech company, is one such partner. In April, the two companies deepened their partnership, adding another $2.8 Bn to an agreement that was initially valued at $500 Mn. 

Such partnership models depend on GPU rental prices holding up. If compute prices fall or older GPUs lose value faster than expected, who absorbs the loss: the neocloud, the customer or the financing partner?

The Jensen Huang Overhang

NVIDIA’s chips, software stack and partnerships shape how quickly new compute capacity comes online. That is one of the reasons The Economist has called it the “central bank of AI”. This also highlights growing concerns about the AI ecosystem’s dependence on NVIDIA.

On November 8, NVIDIA’s board launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be spying for the Chinese government. The NVIDIA board, however, has maintained that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. 

Questions about her alleged links to Chinese intelligence, and what they mean for NVIDIA’s China business, remain open.

For Indian neoclouds, the direct exposure is less about a change in NVIDIA’s leadership and more about their dependence on globally-sourced GPUs and NVIDIA’s software ecosystem. The Government of India has said its compute ecosystem currently relies on globally-sourced GPUs and any change in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics.

There is no evidence yet that the controversy has affected NVIDIA’s relationships with Indian neoclouds. But any fallout for its leadership, China business or financing strategy would hit an ecosystem that leans heavily on NVIDIA’s technology. There are concerns regarding what a potential wider restructuring of NVIDIA might mean for the neocloud business, especially if the build-up of data centres slows down in the US. 

Incidentally, NVIDIA is set to announce its third quarter earnings on November 17, 2026, and this will reveal much more about the underlying numbers for the data centre business. Will the corporate governance issues have an overhang on the stock till then? 

In February this year, the fear was that AI would trigger a SaaSpocalypse. Since then, models have advanced and the opportunities have grown bigger, but the concern now is whether the companies building AI infrastructure can carry the debt and capital commitments needed to keep this boom going.

item.title: Three Workers Die After Inhaling Toxic Gases At Tata’s TN iPhone Factory
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Three contract workers died after allegedly inhaling toxic gases during maintenance work at Tata Electronics’ iPhone manufacturing unit in Tamil…
item.content:encoded:
Three contract workers died after allegedly inhaling toxic gases during maintenance work at Tata Electronics’ iPhone manufacturing unit in Tamil Nadu’s Hosur.

According to Reuters, the incident took place as workers were carrying out cleaning and maintenance work inside a nano-filtration feed tank, which was operated by US-based water treatment company Ecolabs’ subsidiary Nalco Water.

Confirming the development, Nalco Water said that the workers had been employed by one of its sub-contractors. 

“We are deeply saddened by the tragic incident that resulted in the deaths of three workers engaged by a sub-contractor of Nalco Water… This incident occurred in a utility facility, operated by Nalco Water. We are working with the local authorities in the investigation of this incident,” said the company in a statement. 

Sources told the news agency that the deaths, which took place late on Monday, will now be probed by Apple, Tata Electronics and local authorities. Another source reportedly added that an Apple team will visit ​the plant to assist in ​the investigation.

A separate report by Financial Express noted that Tata Electronics will also face an investigation by a joint team of officials from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) and the local Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health (DISH).

As per The New India Express, one of the workers fainted after looking inside the tank and inhaling gas. The other two workers then entered the tank to check on him and also collapsed subsequently due to asphyxiation. 

All three workers were declared dead on arrival at the hospital, the report added. Citing official sources, the report added that there were no proper safety measures in place while handling the effluent treatment plant (ETP). 

While preliminary investigation suggests toxic smoke inhalation, the police have reportedly said the final cause of death would be established after the post-portem. 

This is not the first time that Tata’s iPhone manufacturing unit in Hosur has landed in the middle of a major controversy. In 2024, The latest incident comes nearly two years after the factory was engulfed by a massive fire, which caused injuries to eleven people and halted production.

Not just this, in June this year, the TNPCB had reportedly warned the Tata Hosur unit that the plant would be shut down over alleged wastewater contamination of wells in adjacent farmland. 

Afterwards, Tata Electronics reportedly had said that an independent analysis showed compliance with regulatory norms. The conglomerate later also claimed that ​the pollution control board had dropped further action after the company confirmed that it had addressed all queries.

On top of this, in June itself, a ransomware ​group posted more than 2 Lakh files, including sensitive supplier information, stolen from the same Hosur ⁠iPhone assembly plant on the dark web.

item.title: Matrimony Q2 Profit Soars 2.7X YoY To ₹20.7 Cr, Revenue up 17.6%
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna

item.content:encoded:
Listed matchmaking platform Matrimony’s consolidated net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) skyrocketed 165.4% YoY to ₹20.7 Cr from ₹7.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, profit increased 8.4% from ₹19.1 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Operating revenue rose 17.6% YoY and 3.3% QoQ to ₹134.8 Cr in the quarter under review. In this, revenue from the matchmaking business grew 15.2% YoY to ₹133.9 Cr while revenue from marriage services slid 15% to ₹89 Lakh. 

Including other income of ₹5.9 Cr, the company’s total income for the quarter stood at ₹140.6 Cr. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter rose 2.2% on YoY basis to ₹113.1 Cr. 

Besides the financials, the company also approved the acquisition of 50% stake in astrology based match-making business, Astro-Vision, for INR 8 Cr. With the acquisition, which is set to complete within three months, Matrimony’s stake in the company would rise to 76.9%. This would make Astro-Vision a wholly owned subsidiary of Matrimony. 

The company’s consolidated billing increased 10.7% YoY to ₹131.1 Cr during the quarter, although it declined 3.6% sequentially. The matchmaking business accounted for ₹130.3 Cr of the billing.

During the quarter, Matrimony added 3.02 Lakh paid subscriptions to its matchmaking business, marking a 26.6% YoY increase and an 11.2% rise over the previous quarter.

The company’s matchmaking business reported billing of ₹130.3 Cr, up 10.9% YoY. 

Shares of Matrimony ended today’s trading session 0.14% lower at ₹578.60 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: ShareChat Parent Mohalla Tech’s FY26 Loss Widens 79% To ₹1,978 Cr, Revenue Inches Past ₹1,000 Cr Mark
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Mohalla Tech, the parent of social media platforms ShareChat and Moj, reported a 78.5% YoY increase in its consolidated net…
item.content:encoded:
Mohalla Tech, the parent of social media platforms ShareChat and Moj, reported a 78.5% YoY increase in its consolidated net loss to ₹1,978.4 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 (FY26), weighed down by higher share-based payment expenses, foreign exchange losses and finance costs.

The loss for the fiscal year widened despite a 40.4% jump in operating revenue to ₹1,016.3 Cr from ₹723.4 Cr in FY25. 

Further, the startup also reported an improvement in its operating performance. ShareChat’s management claims that it managed to narrow its FY26 EBITDA loss by 58% YoY to ₹91 Cr and recorded its first EBITDA positive quarter in Q1 FY27. 

The company reported an EBITDA profit of ₹9.5 Cr and a margin of 0.3% in the June quarter. Its EBITDA margin improved to over 2% in Q2 FY27, the management claimed.

QuickTV Subscription Drives Revenue Growth

The startup’s management said its FY26 top line growth was led by the launch of QuickTV, its subscription-based microdrama platform launched in February 2025.

The subscription vertical, which accounts for subscriptions from both Quick TV and Moj (Moj+ and Moj Blue), raked in a revenue of ₹292.7 Cr in the fiscal, accounting for almost 30% of the top line in the fiscal.

Mohalla Tech had counted advertising and livestreaming as its two major pillars for revenue generation since its inception over a decade ago. In the previous fiscal year, it aggressively expanded into monetising the content on its platform amid a growing fervour for microdramas in the Indian content landscape.

Hailed as the “next phase of evolution for the entertainment industry“, Microdrama adoption picked pace in the Indian market early in FY26. ShareChat had launched its vertical microdrama platform, QuickTV, earlier in February 2025. Since then, the app has been downloaded by over 5 Cr users from the Google Play Store.

As its content monetisation took shape, the social media unicorn faced some operational turmoil for its long-set revenue driver — advertising. 

Advertising revenue dipped 13% YoY to ₹251.8 Cr in the fiscal year. This decline came as advertisers from the real money gaming (RMG) stopped promotional spends. To note, ShareChat had already diversified its offerings for clients across FMCG and mid-market advertisers. Hence, it managed to offset the dent anticipated from the RMG ban.

On the other hand, ShareChat’s livestreaming segment grew almost by 9%  YoY  to ₹471.8 Cr. This segment registers revenue from paying users on both ShareChat and Moj platforms.

ShareChat’s FY27 Outlook

For the fiscal year FY27, Mohalla Tech is targeting an EBITDA profit of ₹25 Cr, including at least ₹15 Cr in the second half of FY27.

The startup reported around ₹740 Cr in revenue in the first half of FY27, while its Q2 FY27 annualised revenue run rate reached approximately ₹1,500 Cr. It did not disclose its bottom line performance for the September half of the ongoing fiscal.



To fuel this financial improvement, the startup is expecting both of its content monetisation models — subscription video on demand (SVOD) and advertising-based video on demand (AVOD) — to shoulder its next phase of growth.

ShareChat is expecting its advertising to make a stronger contribution in FY27, growing by 40% YoY. While it is expecting its AVOD revenue to surpass the ₹350 Cr mark, this particular revenue stream touched ₹160 Cr in the first half. 

The management didn’t share any projections for revenue from SVOD in the fiscal. It believes that most Indian internet users are unlikely to pay for microdrama subscriptions, with the number of paying users for the format expected to remain below 100 Mn even as the market matures, making advertising an important monetisation opportunity.

The Microdrama Dillema 

Mohalla Tech’s push into microdrama comes as the format draws growing interest across businesses. 

EloElo Group, the parent of microdrama platform Story TV, recently raised $80 Mn (around ₹756 Cr) in a Series C round led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. The company plans to invest in original content across Indian languages, expand Story TV internationally and strengthen its AI-powered production capabilities. Story TV has more than 5,000 microdramas across six languages, while EloElo claims over 40 Mn monthly active users across its apps.

The space has also attracted startups such as Kuku TV, Flick TV, ReelSaga and Chai Shots, alongside larger platforms including JioHotstar’s Tadka, Zee Entertainment’s Bullet and Amazon MX Player’s MX Fatafat. Businesses and platforms are utilising the short-story format to plug in marketing and products while capitalising on the rise in vertical content consumption.

What’s New: ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech’s consolidated net loss widened 78.5% YoY to ₹1,978.4 Cr in FY26, even as operating revenue jumped 40.4% to ₹1,016.3 Cr.

Why It Matters: Subscription revenue from its microdrama push helped offset declining advertising revenue, while the company narrowed its EBITDA loss by 58%.

The Details: Higher ESOP expenses, forex losses and finance costs weighed on profitability, with total expenses jumping 65.6% YoY. 

However, rising customer acquisition costs and the difficulty of converting free viewers into paying subscribers continue to weigh on the economics of standalone microdrama platforms. For instance, Mohalla Tech said acquiring a user on its free-to-use platform Moj costs around ₹14-15 per download, while acquiring a paying subscriber for QuickTV costs hundreds of rupees, given the latter’s newer brand and subscription paywall. It claimed that competing subscription platforms could be spending upwards of ₹1,000 per subscriber.

Owing to this, platforms like Mohalla Tech are instead banking on advertising revenue and marketing plug-ins to increase monetisation. 

Where Did ShareChat Spend In FY26? 

Mohalla Tech’s total expenses surged 65.6% to ₹3,083 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,862.1 Cr a year earlier.

During its FY26 earnings call, management said the reported loss was largely driven by non-cash and notional accounting items, including provisions for interest on hybrid debt instruments, unrealised foreign exchange losses and ESOP expenses.

Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses under this head more than doubled to ₹959.5 Cr from ₹445.8 Cr in FY25. A large part of the increase came from share-based payments, which climbed 302% to ₹739 Cr in FY26 from ₹183.8 Cr in FY25, following an expansion of the company’s ESOP pool and additional grants to key employees.

Foreign Exchange Losses: Owing to rupee-dollar depreciation, non-cash expenses under this head rose more than fourfold to ₹566.9 Cr from ₹128 Cr in FY25. The increase was largely driven by unrealised forex losses of ₹566 Cr. 

Business Development: Expenses under this head, which usually covers functions like marketing, promotions and customer acquisition, surged 7.7X to ₹334.8 Cr from ₹43.4 Cr in FY26.

item.title: Froncort.AI Raises $2.3 Mn From Google.org To Expand AI-Based Disease Surveillance
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Healthcare AI startup Froncort.AI has secured $2.3 Mn (₹21.5 Cr) in fresh capital from Google’s philanthropic arm, Google.org, to scale…
item.content:encoded:
Healthcare AI startup Froncort.AI has secured $2.3 Mn (₹21.5 Cr) in fresh capital from Google’s philanthropic arm, Google.org, to scale its AI-powered disease surveillance and detection platform.

The support also includes $200K in Google Cloud credits and pro bono technical expertise from Google’s AI specialists.

The funding will help Froncort.AI develop mAI-NETRA, a mobile version of its public health platform AI-NETRA, which uses AI, satellite imagery and government health data to identify higher risk areas for catching infectious diseases. It also guides frontline health workers towards targeted screenings.

The startup is among 15 organisations selected globally for Google.org’s Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation.

Founded in 2024 by physician-scientist Dr Ujjwal Rao, Froncort.AI aims to improve early disease detection by helping frontline health workers enhance their vigil over disease prone areas.

In a validation study conducted with Maharashtra’s state TB programme,Froncort.AI claims that teams using its AI-NETRA identified a similar number of confirmed pulmonary TB cases while screening two-thirds fewer people than conventional methods.

The cost per confirmed case also declined from around $29K to $10K, while 92% of participating frontline workers reported a lower workload.

The platform combines government health programme data with Google’s Earth AI models and local risk indicators, including settlement density, land use, rainfall and flooding, to identify high-risk geographical clusters.

It then converts these insights into ranked work paths, mapping household clusters and builds routes for health workers to follow during field visits.

With the latest funding, Froncort.AI bids to enhance its platform to extend its capabilities across 6 infectious diseases — TB, Leprosy, Malaria, Dengue, Cholera and Leptospirosis.

Froncort.AI also plans to release mAI-NETRA as an open-source blueprint, allowing governments to adopt and adapt the technology for their public health programmes.

Apart from its public health platform, the startup also operates RegDoc, a regulatory technology platform that prepares compliant submissions for clinical research organisations, pharmaceutical companies and medical device manufacturers.

The capital raise comes at a time when AI’s deployment in strengthening India’s public healthcare infrastructure, particularly in areas such as disease surveillance and early diagnosis, is picking up. In a statement issued in February, the government said that India is fundamentally restructuring its public health delivery by integrating AI into a unified strategy. 

“By deploying AI-enabled tools within the National TB Elimination Programme, the National Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Programme, and the Media Disease Surveillance System, the government has empowered non-specialists to perform high-level screenings, resulting in a 27% decline in adverse TB outcomes and over 4,500 outbreak alerts,” the statement read.

It is pertinent to note that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. The IndiaAI Mission is expanding access to compute, supporting indigenous foundation models and providing assistance for AI startups.

Based on Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI funding in India grew 235% YoY, while the number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025.

item.title: Why Gramiyaa Had To Think Like A Supermarket To Win On Quick Commerce
item.dc:creator: Anirudh Trivedi
item.description: It would be naive to think that getting listed on quick commerce platforms is half the battle won. If anything,…
item.content:encoded:
It would be naive to think that getting listed on quick commerce platforms is half the battle won. If anything, that’s where the real battle begins. Building sales velocity, keeping products in stock, managing sky-high platform costs, and, believe it or not, we have barely peered into the abyss.

Gramiyaa, a premium cold-pressed edible oil brand, learnt this the hard way when it boarded the quick commerce bandwagon through Blinkit in 2024.

The first hurdle was affordability. When Gramiyaa finally made it onto quick commerce platforms, it found itself paying nearly twice the commission its national competitors paid. For a small brand already operating on razor-thin margins, that was a steep price to pay just to get a foot in the door.

On top of that, the brand had to set aside a hefty advertising budget, only to burn through it while learning the ropes and figuring out how to make the channel work.

After weathering several battles, including pricing wars between platforms, Gramiyaa has managed to turn the tables. Today, quick commerce is its largest revenue contributor, accounting for 35% of its ₹5 Cr monthly recurring revenue (MRR).

So, how did Gramiyaa navigate these hurdles and turn quick commerce from a costly gamble into its biggest revenue driver?   

In an exclusive conversation for The Quick Commerce Code by Inc42 and Nitro Commerce, Gramiyaa cofounder Mohamed Yaseen shed light on what worked for the brand, how it managed to bring down platform commissions, and the dos and don’ts for emerging D2C brands looking to crack quick commerce.

Why Gramiyaa Had To Look Beyond Its D2C Playbook

Founded by three friends, Mohamed Yaseen, Naveenrajamaran RL and Sibi Manivannan, Gramiyaa’s journey began in 2018 as a local offline business.  

Manivannan’s grandfather ran an oil mill, and Manivannan wanted to breathe new life into the family business, which sold unbranded oil in PET bottles through five to six retail shops in Chennai.

While these shops brought in ₹15-20 Lakh a month, high rents and operating costs ate into the earnings. Besides, each store could only cater to customers in its immediate neighbourhood, leaving little room for growth.

“We had a very stable audience, but were not moving anywhere in terms of growth,” Yaseen told Inc42.

In 2022, Yaseen and Naveenrajamaran RL joined Manivannan, and the three decided to build a new company. Gramiyaa was born.

The founders initially took the D2C route, selling through their own website and setting up small warehouses across four metros to deliver orders within a day. They also looked beyond India, tapping distributors that catered to the Indian diaspora in the US, to take their products overseas. This gave the company a small but high-margin revenue stream.

“However, this was not enough, even though we were doing quite well from our website,” Yaseen said.

As a brand selling only cold-pressed oils, Gramiyaa could attract only so many customers to its own website. To reach a wider audience, the founders decided to list their products on Amazon in November 2022. But this came with an unexpected trade-off. Instead of bringing in only new customers, Amazon began eating into Gramiyaa’s existing D2C sales. Customers who previously bought from its website started ordering through the marketplace, where the brand earned less on every sale.

With its own website offering limited room for growth and Amazon eating into margins, the founders began looking for another avenue to scale, and quick commerce seemed like the obvious next step.

The High Cost Of Breaking Into Quick Commerce

The founders were convinced that quick commerce was a channel they could no longer afford to ignore. But wanting to get on board and actually making it happen were two different things.

For nearly a year, the Gramiyaa founders remained hesitant. The reason? Blinkit and Instamart’s steep commissions. With the brand operating on a razor-thin profit margin of just 2-3%, the cost of entering quick commerce was simply too much.

“This was one year of anxiety and worry. We wanted to do this but couldn’t,” Yaseen recalled.

According to him, if a national cooking oil brand paid a commission of X to a quick commerce channel, a premium oil from a national brand paid about 1.5X. And Gramiyaa, a small and unproven brand, had to pay twice as much. 

However, Yaseen argues that quick commerce is not necessarily more expensive than other distribution channels. Consider a product selling for ₹400, where the brand needs to retain ₹300. The remaining ₹100 goes towards platform margins and advertising on quick commerce. In traditional retail, a similar amount could be absorbed by distributor margins, retailer commissions and the cost of maintaining a sales team.

The bigger challenge for smaller brands, therefore, is not just the cost of distribution, but having enough capital to absorb these expenses before the channel starts generating meaningful sales.

The advertising commitment made the decision even harder. According to Yaseen, brands entering quick commerce with three to four SKUs may be expected to spend ₹5–10 Lakh a month on advertising, even before they have established consistent demand. For a business like Gramiyaa, which was operating on margins of just 2–3% at the time, committing such capital without any assurance of sales was a significant risk.

The decision was eventually made, and the brand got listed on Blinkit in 2024. But after the listing, the channel remained loss-making for nearly six months. According to Yaseen, most brands that do reasonably well on quick commerce barely break even or lose money for six months to a year, and Gramiyaa was no exception. 

“Brands without the capital to absorb this often pause or shut down their quick commerce operations. Thankfully, we had raised funding by the time we went in,” said Yaseen. 

For Gramiyaa, the commissions came down once it proved that demand was pulling customers toward the platforms. When its sales grew from ₹5 Lakh a month to ₹10-15 Lakh and repeat purchases showed that some customers would switch apps, the platforms began treating it more like a large brand.

“Our margins eventually moved gradually closer to what national brands paid,” Yaseen said.

The One-City, One-SKU Strategy Behind Gramiyaa’s Growth

On ecommerce platforms like Amazon, Gramiyaa could ship products to customers anywhere in India from a central warehouse. How well a product ranked depended on how many people clicked on its listing and went on to buy it. Where those customers lived hardly mattered.

Quick commerce, however, is a different ball game altogether. Here, what matters is how quickly a product is sold in a particular neighbourhood.

The challenge becomes clearer at the dark-store level. A slow-moving product may get just one unit of inventory in a particular store. Once a customer buys it, the product can remain unavailable for the next 24–48 hours until it is replenished. Unless the product consistently sells in that locality, platforms have little reason to increase the inventory allocated to it.

This creates a difficult cycle for smaller brands. Limited inventory leads to frequent stockouts, but without sustained sales velocity, securing additional inventory becomes equally difficult.

Yaseen’s rule is that a brand with full confidence in a product in one city should launch there alone, rather than spread across four cities where it is only fairly sure. Within that city, the product has to sell quickly in at least half the dark stores before platforms begin stocking it more deeply. 

“Velocity is everything,” Yaseen said, adding that it was the hardest shift for Gramiyaa’s team. 

Its ecommerce managers were used to optimise listings and found it difficult to plan around availability in each locality. Yaseen took charge of the channel himself and pushed the team to learn how supermarkets and general trade distributors manage stock in each area.

“I believe supermarkets have more in common with running a kirana counter than with running an Amazon listing,” said Yaseen. 

To understand where its products were selling and where they weren’t, Gramiyaa began tracking performance city by city. An intern manually checked pin codes to see where its products appeared in search results and whether they were in stock.

Today, the brand uses tools such as Nitro Commerce to track these metrics, with Yaseen checking the dashboard every morning. 

The exercise revealed two trends: 

  • In some areas, platforms weren’t stocking Gramiyaa’s products at all. 
  • In other areas, demand was strong enough for products to sell out quickly

Armed with these data points, the brand began pushing platforms to stock more units wherever demand was high.

The same data-driven approach helped Gramiyaa optimise advertising spend. Yaseen realised that the company was sometimes paying to promote products that were already ranking well organically on quick commerce apps. By tracking organic and paid share of voice at the SKU and city level, the team began redirecting advertising budgets towards products and locations where additional visibility could make a difference.

This allowed Gramiyaa to make better use of its marketing budget rather than spending indiscriminately across products that were already generating sales.

Over time, product availability became one of Gramiyaa’s most important metrics. The brand now targets 90% on-shelf availability (OSA) and typically achieves 85-90%. According to Yaseen, even the category leader manages only 92-93% in its best month.

And this is where Yaseen sees an opportunity for smaller brands. “When a leading brand runs out of stock, customers often turn to alternatives. If Gramiyaa is available at that moment and its product meets their expectations, it has a chance to win over a new customer,” the cofounder said.

The Big Trade-Off: Pricing, Assortment And Availability

Gramiyaa’s best-selling product on quick commerce is groundnut oil, and its best-selling size is one litre. At one point, it also listed half-litre bottles, a size only a few brands bet on. Yaseen expected it to work as a cheaper trial pack. 

At first, the half-litre pack made up 30% of groundnut oil sales. The team expected that share to fade, but it held. Today, the smaller half-litre packs account for about 15% of total sales volume, which is roughly 30% of its customers. 

This revealed an insight that its young and conscious customers cook occasionally, and others plan their groceries monthly, buy large packs on Amazon, and only use quick commerce when they run out a few days early. 

Adding smaller pack sizes seemed like a good way to attract more customers, but it came with a trade-off. Dark stores have limited shelf space and stock for each brand. If Gramiyaa stocked both half-litre and one-litre bottles, its inventory would be split between the two sizes. A competitor selling only one-litre bottles could stock more units of that size and stay available for longer.

Yaseen decided to prioritise the larger pack, even if it meant losing customers who preferred smaller quantities. 

“If you’re the 20% of customers who won’t buy my brand without the half-litre, I will let go of you. But the 80% who buy my one-litre, I want it repeatedly available for them,” he said, advising new brands to start with a single SKU and choose a product category where larger brands have left a gap.

Not every product decision worked out for Gramiyaa. Of the four oil products the brand introduced on quick commerce, one failed to gain traction because it could not be priced competitively. Yaseen acknowledged that the company had pushed ahead with a product despite knowing it was overpriced and not particularly suited to its core customer base in southern India.

The experience reinforced that expanding an assortment does not necessarily translate into higher sales, especially when dark-store inventory is limited, and a poorly performing SKU can tie up resources better allocated to bestselling products.

Pricing was another headache for Gramiyaa. Yaseen shared that platforms were changing the selling price of their products to match competitors. 

For example, if Instamart offered a discount on one of its SKUs, Blinkit was just going ahead to match that price for the next 20 days to recover its margins. At times, as Yaseen shared, platforms also asked Gramiyaa to cover the price difference. 

“We get caught between two giants fighting to acquire customers,” Yaseen said.

These price fluctuations caused significant losses for Gramiyaa in its early months on quick commerce. It took the company nearly five to six months of negotiations to bring platform margins closer to each other and push back against pricing changes and penalties that were beyond its control.

The pressure was compounded by competition from much larger FMCG players. Yaseen credits Tata with helping popularise the cold-pressed oil category, but its aggressive push has also intensified price competition. For a smaller brand like Gramiyaa, competing on discounts against national players with deeper pockets was never going to be a sustainable strategy.

Yaseen believes that while a popular product such as groundnut oil can help a brand establish itself on quick commerce, its longer-term position will depend on building a presence in more differentiated categories. For Gramiyaa, this makes products such as coconut and sesame oil important, particularly in segments where larger FMCG companies may not be competing as aggressively.

Today, Yaseen shared, Gramiyaa does not need to rely heavily on discounts to drive sales. At ₹350-750, a single one-litre bottle is expensive enough to qualify for a platform’s free delivery threshold. 

The purchasing behaviour also works in Gramiyaa’s favour. According to Yaseen, its customers typically reorder every 40–45 days and buy an average of 1.3-1.4 products per order, while ₹350 is an effective price point for the brand on quick commerce.

Unlike lower-ticket products that may depend on being added to a larger grocery basket, a single bottle of Gramiyaa’s oil can account for a substantial portion of the order value. Combined with repeat demand, this gives the brand an advantage in building consistent sales velocity.

Gramiyaa’s Next Quick Commerce Test

Gramiyaa reported ₹18 Cr in revenue in FY25, which grew 61.1% to ₹29 Cr in FY26, with quick commerce the largest channel at 35%, or about ₹10.15 Cr. But this growth has come at the expense of profit.

According to Yaseen, the brand was profitable in FY25. As of now, remaining profitable is the least of its concerns, as the company expects to burn for brand visibility and new channels. 

Recently, Gramiyaa raised ₹21 Cr as part of its ongoing Series A fundraise led by Optiscape Network Holdings, Homegrown Ventures, Campus Fund and others. The funds would be used to fuel its expansion in Tier II markets. 

For Gramiyaa, the next phase of quick commerce growth lies beyond India’s metros. Yaseen believes the channel’s appeal in Tier II cities is somewhat different from that in larger markets. Rather than simply promising delivery within minutes, quick-commerce platforms are increasingly offering consumers access to products that may not be readily available at their neighbourhood kirana stores.

For a premium cold-pressed oil brand with limited offline distribution in these markets, that creates an opportunity to reach customers who might otherwise struggle to find its products locally.

The company expects quick commerce to remain its largest revenue channel as it expands into these markets. However, Yaseen acknowledges that the next phase will depend on how successfully platforms penetrate smaller cities, particularly as growth in established metro markets begins to moderate.

However, when asked about platforms prioritising their own labels over D2C brands, Yaseen does not see much competition there, as the brand operates in the premium category, selling to customers who prefer quality over price. 

But for founders considering the channel, Yaseen’s advice is to wait. 

“Quick commerce should be built only after a brand has a core business on its website or an ecommerce platform like Amazon. They need to know their hero products, figure out pricing, and have strong liquidity from another channel or cash flow,” the cofounder stated, outlining the imperatives for newer brands stuck at the bottom of the pyramid. 

Gramiyaa avoided this trap, but the harder test of holding its position in Tier II cities is yet to come. Can it sustain demand in markets where premium purchases often take a backseat to essential spending?

AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India managing director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its president and chief business officer (CBO), as it looks to strengthen its enterprise and government business and scale the commercial deployment of its AI technology.

In his new role, Sreedharan will lead Sarvam’s business across enterprises and government institutions while expanding its engagement with digital-native companies, developers and partners. He will also oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations, the company said in a blog post.

Sreedharan will also join the company’s board of directors.

Before joining Sarvam, Sreedharan  served as MD of Google Cloud India for over a year. Across a career spanning about 35 years, he has served across companies like Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others.

His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to move beyond developing indigenous AI models and build a larger enterprise business around its technology.

The startup said it provides its full-stack AI offerings to over 100 enterprises and government institutions.  “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale,” the startup said. 

Sarvam AI’s Push To Build The India Stack

Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure, and enterprise applications. Its offerings target businesses and government agencies seeking tools tailored to Indian languages, data-security requirements, and local use cases.

The new CBO appointment comes shortly after Sarvam expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Prism. The “System One” decision model built on top of Sarvam AI’s Sarvam 105B foundation model. Rather than generating open-ended text token-by-token like a conventional LLM, it evaluates a given context, a question, and a predefined list of options in a single processing pass to return calibrated probabilities for each choice.

The startup has also released several other models in recent months, including Sarvam Vision 2.1, a vision-language model for processing documents and recognising text in Indian languages, and Saaras V4, its speech-to-text model. In October, it launched Bulbul V4 Flash, a text-to-speech model for generating natural speech across Indian languages.

Earlier this year, Sarvam raised $234 Mn in the first close of its $300 Mn Series B funding round, which valued the company at $1.5 Bn. The unicorn minting round saw participation from investors HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

It is now reportedly in talks with Nasdaq-listed IT services company Cognizant Technology Solutions to raise further funds for the round. It is looking to raise around $300 Mn at a valuation of around $3.5 Bn to $4 Bn.

item.title: InMobi Secures Naming Rights For Bengaluru’s Ibbaluru Metro Station For ₹65 Cr
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Ahead of its long due IPO, adtech unicorn InMobi has bolstered its marketing by securing a naming rights for Bengaluru’s…
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of its long due IPO, adtech unicorn InMobi has bolstered its marketing by securing a naming rights for Bengaluru’s Ibbaluru Metro Station for the next 30 years via a ₹65 Cr deal.

The partnership will see InMobi support Namma Metro over a 30-year concession, and Ibbaluru Metro Station will be known as InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station.

“Bengaluru is one of the world’s leading technology hubs. InMobi was born here, and over the last 18 years, we’ve grown alongside the city, continuing to build from India for the world. This partnership is our way of giving back to the city that gave us our start,” the company said in a statement. 

The deal will contribute to BMRCL’s non-fare revenue, which includes income from commercial activities such as station branding and advertising, alongside its core passenger fare collections. BMRCL said the partnership would support metro infrastructure development and encourage more corporate participation in the city’s public transport ecosystem.

The naming-rights deal comes as InMobi continues to work towards a public listing in India, a plan first reported over two years ago. In July 2024, reports said the company was targeting a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. However, the proposed timeline has since slipped, with InMobi yet to file its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP).

The delay in the proposed listing has coincided with changes in InMobi’s shareholding structure.

In December 2025, InMobi’s cofounders bought back around 25-30% stake from early investor SoftBank, bringing the latter’s holding down from approximately 35% to less than 8%. The transaction was backed by $350 Mn in debt raised from Varde Partners, Elham Credit Partners and SeaTown Holdings.

The reshuffle in InMobi’s cap table continued in 2026, with private equity firm True North reportedly acquiring a 2-3% stake through a secondary transaction valued at around $50-60 Mn. The deal also provided partial exits to some early investors.

Alongside these shareholder transactions, InMobi has been putting the banking team in place for its proposed listing. The company has appointed JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital as merchant bankers for the IPO. Earlier reports pegged the proposed issue at around $1 Bn, although subsequent valuation estimates have varied.

While the IPO remains a work in progress, InMobi has continued to expand its advertising technology capabilities through acquisitions. In May 2026, the company acquired San Francisco-based mobile app marketing and analytics platform MobileAction to strengthen its capabilities in app discovery, user acquisition and advertising optimisation.

item.title: OpenAI Deploys Control Room With 35-Second Kill Switch Amid Security Concerns
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Amid growing threats of rogue AI agents, ChatGPT parent OpenAI has developed and deployed Control Room, a centralised system to…
item.content:encoded:
Amid growing threats of rogue AI agents, ChatGPT parent OpenAI has developed and deployed Control Room, a centralised system to monitor its AI research workloads and stop models from generating output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene.

In a blog post, the company noted that all advanced AI training jobs are monitored by a separate AI model that flags potentially problematic behaviour. If an issue is detected, the monitoring system can instruct the Control Room to terminate the job. 

Control Room then blocks any further inference requests associated with that job ID, preventing the model from generating additional output across any model or engine. If a job has been terminated, Control Room denies the request, preventing further model output. The restriction applies across all models and inference engines associated with that job.

However, stopping a job is not instantaneous. Control Room can take up to 35 seconds to prevent further model output after receiving an instruction to intervene. This delay is caused by a caching layer used to handle the volume of inference requests. OpenAI said it is working to bring the response time down to zero.

The system works alongside its existing misalignment monitoring systems and allows researchers to stop or pause a job when potential safety or security concerns arise. It tracks workloads across OpenAI’s research infrastructure, including model training, evaluations, agentic sampling and data processing.

The company said the system is already deployed across its research infrastructure, where the need for such safeguards is greatest. Its external model-serving infrastructure, meanwhile, is more centralised and already has operational mechanisms to take down model deployments when required.

OpenAI cited a recent incident in which one of its AI agents used DNS to reach an external chatbot as an example of an issue detected by its monitoring systems.

The company has rolled out the fail-closed mechanism across its frontier model research workloads and expects to extend it to all remaining research workloads over the following days.

AI Agent Behaviour Under Scrutiny

The development comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents and their ability to act beyond their intended instructions.

Last month, the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, reported unusual activity across Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects involving systems it believed were operated by OpenAI.

The activity included unauthorised edits, attempts to use Wikimedia services as a proxy and millions of automated requests. While most edits were confined to sandbox environments and were not visible to readers, Wikimedia also flagged changes to the configuration of a citation tool that it suspected could have been intended to retrieve data from external services.

A similar concern emerged in July 2026, when OpenAI’s autonomous AI evaluation agents reportedly escaped sandboxed environments during cybersecurity benchmark tests under ExploitGym. The agents subsequently accessed the production infrastructure of AI development platform Hugging Face. They reportedly included an internal research model and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Taken together, these incidents highlight the challenges of containing AI agents that can independently execute tasks, interact with external systems and potentially operate beyond their intended boundaries.

These developments come as ChatGPT continues to expand its presence in India, which has emerged as its largest market globally by weekly active users. Its user base in the country has doubled since January 2026.
